name: Patria Grande
summary: Patria Grande is the idea of a shared homeland uniting the Spanish-speaking (and by extension all Latin American) nations in one community, in the tradition of Bolivar and San Martin and as developed by Manuel Ugarte. It holds that the region's fragmentation lets outside powers, above all the United States, dominate it, so sovereignty depends on political and economic integration. Today it is used mostly by left and nationalist leaders such as Lula, Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner and Chavez-era Bolivarians.
scope: Ugarte's anti-imperialist Latin American unity (La Patria Grande, 1922) and the Bolivarian integration heritage as invoked by present-day left governments (Mercosur, UNASUR, CELAC, ALBA). It is a regional unity idea rather than a full programme, so positions on domestic economy, morals and institutions are mostly inferred from its left-leaning backers and given low confidence.

sources.usedFor: Sovereignty, self-sufficiency, participatory democracy and corruption themes in the Bolivarian version.

worker-ownership.rationale: Latin American cooperativism influenced Chavez's Bolivarianism, but adherents are split and it is not core.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Nothing in the concept addresses surveillance; adherents are split.

strong-leader.rationale: Chavista strands favor strong personalist leadership while others (Lula, Vazquez) do not; split.

state-harmful.rationale: The project is built on states and their confederation, and Bolivarianism assigns the state a central role; anarchism is foreign to it.

decide-locally.rationale: Bolivar and Ugarte stress continental union over fragmentation, so powers lean toward larger bodies; but local autonomy is not rejected explicitly.

traditional-family.rationale: Backers include both secular leftists and Catholic figures such as Pope Francis, so split.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Split between progressive leaders and Catholic/traditional supporters; not part of the concept.

abortion-legal.rationale: Split: Kirchner-style progressives versus Catholic supporters such as Pope Francis.

more-religion-public.rationale: Pope Francis invokes the homeland but the concept is not religious; split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Preserving a shared Latin American cultural heritage is central, though at the continental rather than national level.

gradual-change.rationale: Integration has proceeded through treaties and blocs like Mercosur, but the independence heritage is revolutionary; split.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Supports regional bodies (Mercosur, CELAC, UNASUR) but is wary of Northern-dominated global ones; genuinely mixed.

free-trade.rationale: Ugarte's critique targeted foreign economic domination; modern backers favor regional integration and sovereignty over liberal free trade, though they back intra-regional trade.

nation-first.rationale: Core aim is shared homeland and regional cooperation, so putting a single country ahead of cooperation runs against it, though sovereignty versus outside powers is valued.

limit-growth.rationale: Chavista programs prioritize development and resource use; degrowth is not part of it.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Nuclear energy is outside the concept; backer governments (Argentina, Brazil) have nuclear programs but others do not.

revolution-justified.rationale: The movement claims the independence revolutions of Bolivar and San Martin and Chavez's Bolivarian revolution as models.

experts-over-public.rationale: Bolivarianism emphasizes grassroots participation and popular votes over technocracy.

central-planning.rationale: Chavista strands favor planning and self-sufficiency while others keep mixed markets; split.

basic-income.rationale: Unconditional income is not part of the idea; backers are split between conditional transfers and other models.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Ugarte attacked dependence of exporting oligarchies; Bolivarianism seeks economic self-sufficiency and sovereignty, so protecting domestic industry is consistent.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Backers reform capitalism but do not seek to abolish money.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Peronist backers have used corporatist bargaining, others not; split.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Rebelion account links Patria Grande progress to elections and democratic recovery; single-party rule is not part of it.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Bolivar concluded Americans would prefer republics to kingdoms, and the independence tradition is republican.

democracy-best.rationale: Regional progress is linked to elections and democratic recovery in the source, though Chavista strands are ambivalent about liberal constraints.

workers-councils.rationale: Participatory structures are favored but not councils replacing parliaments.

political-violence-never.rationale: Independence wars and revolutionary heritage are celebrated, though contemporary leaders emphasize diplomacy.

war-builds-character.rationale: Lula and others stress peaceful integration; no glorification of war.

separate-church-state.rationale: Split between secular leftists and religious supporters.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Not part of the concept; supporters mostly favor secular law despite Catholic voices.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The homeland is conceived across shared history and culture including Indigenous peoples, not a single ethnic group.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Ugarte blended socialism with nationalism, stressing the national struggle against imperialism over class alone; split.

civilizational-union.rationale: Core claim: peoples with shared roots, history and language of Spanish America should unite in a common homeland.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Bolivarianism stresses patriotic service and solidarity.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Chavez stressed a national ethic of patriotic service but also rights; split.

restore-past-order.rationale: Looks to a historic unity project but aims at progress through integration; not restorationist.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The movement is explicitly ideological in its Bolivarian and anti-imperialist tradition.

production-for-use.rationale: Self-sufficiency in food and goods is stressed, but no stance on profit.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Ugarte was a socialist but later focused on imperialism; contemporary backers split.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Not a Patria Grande position; Ugarte left party socialism.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Ugarte denounced imperialism and voted against colonialist thesis in Stuttgart, but linked it to US expansion, not capitalism generally.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Links progress to elections and voice.

media-academia-power.rationale: Ugarte complained of marginalization by universities and academies, but not a thesis about media power.

total-state.rationale: Democratic framing in sources; no total state.

national-rebirth.rationale: Bolivarian rhetoric of revolution and rebirth appears, but not decadence theory.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Ugarte complained of marginalization by institutions, but there is no epistemic doctrine.

single-common-good.rationale: The idea has no theory of a single rational common good; backers include pluralist democrats and Catholic thinkers.

economic-freedom.rationale: Ugarte saw economic domination by foreign capital as the main threat, not an absence of economic freedom.

national-self-determination.rationale: Sovereignty and a second independence are core, though at the continental level.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The concept is neutral on faith versus reason; Pope Francis and secular leftists both invoke it.

class-collaboration.rationale: Ugarte linked socialist and nationalist outlooks; Peronist strands favor class collaboration while others do not.

dominated-front.rationale: Core: Latin American countries dominated by outside powers should unite in a common front; Peron's 'united or dominated' and Ugarte's anti-imperialist union.

workers-nation.rationale: Ugarte combined socialist internationalism with nationalism; split.

ban-interest.rationale: Prohibiting interest is not part of Latin American unity thought; left backers want credit access, not bans.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Chavista strands treat natural resources as sovereign wealth to be used; split but lean yes.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Backers split between secular leftists and religious supporters such as Pope Francis, and the sources are silent.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Republican independence tradition rests on popular sovereignty.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The framing is solidarity among peoples against domination, not competition as a motor of progress.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Unidos o dominados: freedom as absence of foreign domination is central, though applied to nations.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Ugarte blamed foreign domination and oligarchies.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Unity of diverse peoples is the aim.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Sortition has no place in the sources, whose republican tradition relies on elections.

party-commands-army.rationale: The sources do not propose party control of armed forces; republican tradition favors state control.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The open-doors attitude toward regional peoples (Lula's remark) opposes long waiting periods, though only loosely.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party discipline is not an issue of the sources and varies among backers' parties.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Regional integration through Mercosur, UNASUR and CELAC is the central aim, but these are intergovernmental bodies, and the sources do not describe binding supranational institutions of the EU kind.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Ugarte was neutralist in WWI; ambiguous.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Chavismo and others pursued it, others disagree.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Opposes US military bases but favors regional defense cooperation; split.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Banning rentals has no basis in the sources and is not a backer position.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The sources celebrate Indigenous solidarity but do not rank rural over urban life morally.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Reuniting the fragments of Spanish America is central to Bolivar and Ugarte, but the region split in the independence wars rather than along a border drawn by an outside power, and Ugarte sought a confederation more than one state.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Ugarte complained of marginalization by academies, but there is no stated claim about educated people's detachment.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Backers split between progressive governments and Catholic supporters; the unity sources are silent.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Open-doors regional citizenship leans to territorial and regional rights.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Millian eccentricity and conformity are not a theme of the sources; solidarity themes lean against but are not explicit.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Ugarte stressed that political independence is hollow under foreign economic domination and oligarchies; second independence rhetoric of Castro and Chavez.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Presidential systems dominate the region, and the sources do not call for a nonpartisan symbolic head of state.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Republican tradition; Bolivar warned against tyranny.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Bolivar sought a middle between extremes, but this is not a doctrine.

leader-cult.rationale: Chavismo and Peronism honor leaders heavily; others do not; split.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a league, federation, cooperation or unity in general, not one state, which this statement now asks.

reviewHistory.rationale: Peoples sharing language family and ancestry should unite: Ugarte's call for union of Hispanic America from shared roots, history and culture.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a league, federation, cooperation or unity in general, not one state, which this statement now asks.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Ugarte was a socialist but Patria Grande is not Marxist doctrine.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Chavista strands favor majoritarianism; others not.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Foquismo is a Cuban doctrine; Castro's name appears among backers, but Ugarte and the unity concept do not endorse it.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Republican independence tradition rejects colonial peninsular privileges; Bolivar criticized laws favoring Spanish-born.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Ugarte stressed Latin American cultural identity and own thought against domination.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Ugarte voted at Stuttgart against the thesis supporting colonialism of civilized countries.

delink-world-market.rationale: Backers seek regional integration, Mercosur and trade, not full delinking.

elective-rulers.rationale: Bolivar concluded republics are preferred over kingdoms, rejecting hereditary rule.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Independence tradition justified resistance to oppressive rule; Bolivar cited tyrants governing a desert.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The Frankfurt-style critique of mass culture is not part of the sources; Ugarte did stress cultural defense, but not this claim.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Ugarte criticised exporting oligarchies and foreign domination; dependency-style claims are common among backers.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Bolivian MAS did this; not a general stance.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A US historiographical question absent from the sources.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Ugarte urged independent Latin American thought rather than imported models.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Peronist and Chavista strands favored military roles; others not.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Ugarte attacked foreign economic domination; sovereignty over resources.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about community or state ownership of land, and the statement now asks only whether a right to hold land should end when the holder stops using it.

reviewHistory.rationale: Land belonging to the community or nation is a feature of some Andean traditions but not a stated tenet of Patria Grande.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about community or state ownership of land, and the statement now asks only whether a right to hold land should end when the holder stops using it.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Sovereignty framing; Bolivarian governments did this.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Racial ranking contradicts the solidarity of mixed, shared peoples at the heart of the concept; Ugarte-inspired accounts celebrate Indigenous and shared heritage.

local-production.rationale: The concept stresses regional integration and self-sufficiency, not local production specifically.

informal-organisation.rationale: The idea is pursued through governments and institutions such as Mercosur, UNASUR, CELAC and ALBA, not small informal groups.

religious-nation.rationale: The community is defined by language, history and shared colonial past, not religion; Bolivar favoured republics over religious authority.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The idea exists to resist outside domination of Latin America, summed up as 'unidos o dominados'.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Central: the concept is anti-imperialist and holds that outside powers exploit a fragmented region, which is the relationship the statement describes.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Closely tied to its anti-US sovereignty aim: UNASUR and CELAC were built to act as a regional bloc independent of US-led alliances.

reification.rationale: A unity idea with no stated theory of market social relations; left backers vary in how far they hold this.

racial-franchise.rationale: Bolivar's Carta de Jamaica and Ugarte frame unity around a mixed, shared Latin American people, which is incompatible with an ethnic franchise.

term-limits.rationale: Bolivar favoured strong long-serving executives and Chavez-era Bolivarians removed limits, while other backers support them; no settled view.

gm-crops.rationale: Contested among backers: some governments embrace GM crops, others ban them.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Ugarte and the Bolivarian tradition treat the Spanish-speaking nations, divided by state borders, as one patria sharing language and history.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Ugarte held that outside powers, above all the United States, exploit Latin America's fragmentation to dominate it, and Balkanisation is the core grievance.

pollution-taxes.rationale: A regional unity idea with no stated environmental programme; its backers are split between extractivist and green positions.

arms-reduction.rationale: Regional integration bodies such as UNASUR promote peace and joint defence councils, but the idea also treats defence of sovereignty as vital; adherents are split.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Patria Grande rests on the argument that a united region resists domination, and CELAC and ALBA are used to seek a fairer economic order for the region.

sacred-nation.rationale: The nation here is the continental homeland of Bolivar and San Martin, an enduring community, though the sources do not call it sacred.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Patria Grande is a regional-unity idea with no stated position on union membership; its left backers are split between labour protection and flexibility.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Integration backers claim democratic legitimacy and also stress social outcomes and sovereignty; the idea does not settle this and adherents are split.

women-suffrage.rationale: Women's political equality is accepted across Latin American left and nationalist movements that invoke Patria Grande, and has been law across the region for decades.

defend-planned-state.rationale: The idea concerns regional unity and takes no position; Bolivarian backers are split between defending planned states such as Cuba and criticising them.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The idea is about regional unity and does not address resource ownership theory; its backers are split between common-ownership and national-control views.

self-ownership.rationale: Patria Grande does not address self-ownership; its left backers are split between liberal-individual and collective emphases.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The idea does not address denominational politics and Latin American backers are split.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Patria Grande offers no stated view of technology versus ancestral values; backers are split.

national-resource-control.rationale: Ugarte and later integrationists see foreign control of resources as the core of imperial domination and want regional or national sovereignty over them.

multipolar-world.rationale: Patria Grande seeks a united region strong enough to resist domination by one outside power, and its modern backers frame this as a multipolar order.

missingStatements.text: Nations that were once one empire or share a colonial history should unite in a regional confederation to resist domination by outside powers.
missingStatements.rationale: Ugarte called for a continental confederation against Pan-American and Anglo-Saxon imperialism, following Bolivar and San Martin.

missingStatements.text: One large neighbouring power's political and economic influence over a region is the main threat to the region's independence.
missingStatements.rationale: Ugarte located the imperialist danger in United States political, cultural and economic action, unlike Justo who stressed Britain.

notes: Thin as a standalone ideology: most answers are inferred from the left-leaning leaders who use the term and are low confidence, so the inclusion check may exclude it. Backers range from Catholic figures to Marxist-influenced socialists.
